Article Title: Apple may launch its rival to Meta Ray Ban smart glass at WWDC 2027: Report
Article Text:
Apple may focus on privacy as a key feature for its smart glasses

Apple’s smart glass may feature a different design

Apple's Mac plan for the next two years revealed

Apple is reportedly planning to unveil its first smart glasses next year. According to a Bloomberg report, the company may launch its first smart glass at Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) 2027 with privacy in focus. In the latest edition of PowerOn newsletter, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said that for smart glasses, Apple is prototyping "a slew of new hardware and software-related privacy features" that are currently not available on any products. While he did not reveal any key feature of the device, Gurman said that Apple’s marketing may focus on privacy features for its smart glasses compared to rival products like the Meta Ray-Bans.Apple is exploring different designs for its future smart glasses. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the company has considered making a version with cameras that help power AI features but do not allow users to take photos or record videos.Apple has also tested prototypes without any cameras at all, the newsletter states. The idea is to address privacy concerns, as some people worry about being secretly recorded by smart glasses.Even so, Mark Gurman said the most likely version will include cameras. Apple is expected to add privacy features that match the company's strong focus on protecting users.Like Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses, Apple's device is also expected to include speakers and microphones. These would let users listen to music, make phone calls and hear Siri notifications. Apple is reportedly aiming to launch the smart glasses in late 2027.In another news, Apple is preparing to refresh every Mac it sells across this fall and the next two years. A Bloomberg report stated that the wave may start with a low-end 14-inch MacBook Pro running the new M6 chip and the first new iMacs in two years—both finished in development, both waiting on a fall launch window. Internally they carry the codenames J804, J833 and J834.
Article Summary: Apple may launch its first smart glass at Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) 2027 with privacy in focus. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said Apple is prototyping "a slew of new hardware and software-related privacy features" that are currently not available on any products.

Article Title: Read letter that has Satya Nadella, Sundar Pichai, Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Sam Altman and many other CEOs of biggest American technology companies saying: 'This has our full support'
Article Text:
Arguments for openness

Access : Startups and universities can build on advanced models without prohibitive costs.

: Startups and universities can build on advanced models without prohibitive costs. Competition : Rivalry across developers, chips, and services drives innovation and lowers costs.

: Rivalry across developers, chips, and services drives innovation and lowers costs. Control : Organizations avoid lock-in and retain ownership of their AI capabilities.

: Organizations avoid lock-in and retain ownership of their AI capabilities. Security: Transparency allows vulnerabilities to be identified and remediated across many teams.

Read the letter here

Open Weights and American AI Leadership

July 24, 2026

In the 1980s, early open-source software pioneers challenged the prevailing belief that software would advance only if companies kept tight control over their code. This movement pushed for a transparent ecosystem where developers around the world could study, modify, and improve software. Software developed by the open-source community now supports most of the internet and underlies systems used by the world’s largest technology companies, as well as the U.S. military and federal agencies conducting scientific research, cybersecurity, and other critical missions. Open source did more than lower the cost of software; it created a shared foundation of knowledge on which generations of American engineers and entrepreneurs built their institutional sovereignty.

The United States now faces a similar choice with artificial intelligence. Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector. This is essential for creating opportunities for innovation and prosperity across the country. It requires expanding access to AI, encouraging competition, robust application layers, and giving Americans greater control over the technology they rely on. Open weight models—AI models that anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure—are an important part of that foundation because they make advanced AI more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.

Open weights expand access to the AI economy. Startups, established businesses, universities, and public institutions can build on advanced models without training one from scratch or paying frontier-model prices for every task. Open weights let every organization match the right model to the right job at the right cost, reserving frontier-scale capability for genuine frontier problems and running efficient, specialized models everywhere else. That discipline is what will make AI economically sustainable as its use scales into the billions of everyday tasks. America wins the AI era by diffusing it into the workflows of factories, hospitals, farms, classrooms, and main street businesses.

Open weights also strengthen competition and competition is what keeps the gains of AI broadly shared rather than concentrated in a few hands. By allowing many organizations to build, adapt, and deploy advanced models, open weights create rivalry not only among model developers but across cloud chips, applications, and services. That competition spurs innovation, drives down costs, and distributes the benefits of AI broadly across our economy.

Open weights also give customers greater control. As organizations invest in AI, they want to know that they will not become locked into a single provider or lose the knowledge and capabilities they build over time. Open weight models help provide that assurance by allowing organizations to control their own data, evaluate and adapt models to their own needs, and deploy them wherever their business requirements demand. And as organizations create value with AI, open weights allow them to own that value through self-improving models, specialized capabilities, and accumulated knowledge that drive American sovereignty and prosperity.

To be sure, open weights carry real and distinct risks. Once released, the weights are beyond the original developer’s control, and modified versions are difficult to trace or reverse. But the right response to this risk is not to prohibit open weights. In a world where cybersecurity attackers use advanced AI, defenders need access to models with comparable capabilities so they can detect, simulate, and respond to emerging threats. Open models broaden defensive capability, increase transparency, and allow vulnerabilities to be discovered and remediated across many teams.

In fact, openness may be one of the most important paths to AI safety and security. Relying solely on closed models is not inherently safe: they can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect. And concentrating advanced AI capabilities behind a small number of closed models compounds that risk. It results in a small number of single points of failure, weakens competition, and leaves critical technology in the hands of a few providers. Open weight models, on the other hand, allow a broad community of researchers and developers to examine their behavior, identify vulnerabilities, develop safeguards, and improve them over time. Just as open-source software demonstrated that transparency can be more secure than obscurity, AI safety may depend on giving more people the ability to test and strengthen the models on which society relies. It allows for rigorous benchmarking and evaluation, red teaming, and protections tied to real and demonstrated harms rather than assuming that closed systems are safer by default.

A strong AI ecosystem is not a foregone conclusion. Policymakers have an important opportunity to act. This includes expanding access to compute for startups and researchers, investing in shared training assets (datasets, tools, evaluation frameworks), and keeping the frontier plural by avoiding premature restrictions on open models that stifle competition or drive innovation overseas. These measures must also look at how strong application layers can expand sovereign use of AI across the economy.

In shaping this ecosystem, policymakers should be careful not to conflate legitimate model-development techniques with misappropriation. Distillation, or the practice of using one model’s outputs to help train or improve another, is a widely used technique for model improvement, evaluation, and validation. It reflects a long tradition of learning from, building upon, and improving existing technologies, a tradition that has helped drive innovation since the rise of the open-source software movement. By contrast, unlawful efforts to extract value from closed models raise legitimate concerns. Those concerns should be addressed through targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping restrictions on techniques that play an important role in AI innovation.

The age of AI can be one of prosperity. With the right choices, open weight AI can expand opportunity, strengthen competition, extend American technological leadership, mitigate risk, and ensure that the benefits of this extraordinary technology are shared broadly across our economy. That future is worth building, and the United States should lead in building it.

A coalition of 25 leading technology companies and organisations has published a joint letter titled Open Weights and American AI Leadership recently, is urging policymakers to embrace open-weight AI models. The letter argues that America’s AI leadership depends not on a single frontier model but on building a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses across industries. It highlights how open weights AI models that anyone can download, inspect, and run expand access, spur competition, and give greater control to organisations over their data and capabilities. The letter has also drawn endorsements from the biggest names in technology.Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote, “Open-weight models are essential to a healthy AI ecosystem. Together with others across our industry, we are outlining a path for open-weight models to strengthen American competitiveness and expand economic opportunity, while protecting national security,” supporting the letter on X. Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google, posted, “Very happy to support this on behalf of Google. We have long benefited from open source, are big contributors to open source and in fact have consistently made open weights models with Gemma available from @GoogleDeepMind @demishassabis .Onwards!”OpenAI’s Sam Altman also endorsed the letter and wrote on X, “i want the US to win in AI both in open source and proprietary models, and i am glad to see this.” “This has my full support,” added Elon Musk . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang joined the chorus, highlighting the importance of open-weight AI for startups, researchers, and public institutions and posted on X, “For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter. AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty. The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.”The coalition’s letter outlines several benefits of open weights:
Article Summary: Open Weights and American AI Leadership will be judged by whether the U.S. builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector. It requires expanding access to AI, encouraging competition, robust application layers, and giving Americans greater control over technology they rely on.

Article Title: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is hiring software engineers, designers, researchers for his 'tech crew': Here's what the job actually is
Article Text:
NYC mayor wants his ‘tech crew’ to build city software from inside the agency



New York City is betting that in-house tech teams will ship faster and cost less



New York City has opened applications for a new kind of government job. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Monday that the city is recruiting software engineers, product designers, product managers, user researchers, service designers and data experts to staff what he is calling Public Interest Technology Crews—PIT Crews, a pun the mayor committed to by rolling up to the Coney Island go-kart track to make the announcement.The hiring is funded and specific. A City Hall spokesperson confirmed around 30 full-time roles across four crews, supported by $5.24 million in baseline funding in the mayor's new fiscal budget. The listings are live at nyc.gov/pitcrew.A PIT Crew is a mixed team—engineers, designers, product managers, user researchers and data experts—placed alongside staff at a city agency rather than parked in a separate technology department. The crew works with that agency and with New Yorkers to design, build and launch a digital tool, then learn from how people actually use it. The mayor's office describes the timeline as months rather than years, which is the entire premise of the model.Five crews are planned. One handles the Click to Cancel complaint portal, three are attached to Mamdani's affordability and public excellence agenda, and a fifth is being developed with support from The Rockefeller Foundation through the Mayor's Fund to Advance New York City.Zohran Mamdani’s PIT crew’s first assignment is a complaint portal with teethCrew one works with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection on an online portal where New Yorkers can report companies that make subscriptions near-impossible to cancel. It supports the Click to Cancel rule Mamdani announced last week, which requires businesses to offer the same exit route customers used to sign up. Enforcement begins October 1, and the junk fees ban lands January 1, 2027.The portal is built to do two things at once—give individual New Yorkers a route to recourse, and give City Hall a running database of repeat offenders.Chief Technology Officer and OTI Commissioner Lisa Gelobter framed the roles around a shift in what government technology now is. Every service has a digital surface, she argued, and every confusing step in that surface erodes trust. Her operating instruction for the crews is user first, always, with outcomes weighted over outputs.There is a politics to the hiring as well. NYC-DSA's Tech Action organisers backed the announcement as a choice to build capacity inside government rather than route taxpayer money to consultancies and big tech vendors. BetaNYC's Noel Hidalgo made the cost version of the same argument—in-house teams that deliver faster and cheaper than the outsourced alternative."New Yorkers should not be forced to navigate systems that are confusing, outdated and burdened by bureaucracy," Mamdani said. "The PIT Crew turns that model on its head."Public Interest Technology took shape as a field in the 2010s on a fairly unglamorous premise: government software is usually bad, and fixing it is a staffing and usability problem more than an engineering one. The recruitment page leans into that, pitching the work rather than the salary—the goal, it says, is to make interacting with government dignified and delightful for every New Yorker.
Article Summary: New York City launches Public Interest Technology Crews (PIT Crews) Crews will build city software from inside the agency rather than in a separate department. Hiring is funded by $5.24 million in the mayor's new fiscal budget.

Article Title: YouTube will now help creators make thumbnails easily using AI
Article Text:
Custom thumbnails arrive for YouTube Shorts



Generate custom thumbnails with ‘ Ask Studio ’



YouTube has announced a series of updates that are designed to simplify and speed up the thumbnail creation process, giving creators more control over how their content appears across the platform. The video-sharing giant is introducing custom thumbnail options for YouTube Shorts and rolling out conversational AI-generated thumbnails for long-form videos directly within its Studio dashboard.The changes aim to help creators save valuable production time while boosting viewer engagement and click-through rates, the company said in an announcement.In response to one of its most frequently requested features, YouTube said that it is expanding thumbnail customization for its short-form video feed.Custom Shorts uploads: YouTube Partner Program creators can now upload fully custom thumbnail images for their Shorts, offering greater control over branding and visual presentation. The company said that it plans to expand this capability to more creators in the coming months.Desktop frame selection: Creators uploading Shorts via desktop can now choose from three automatically suggested thumbnail frames, matching a feature long available for standard long-form videos.Creators can still select any precise video frame using the YouTube mobile app.For long-form video creators, YouTube is bringing direct thumbnail generation into Ask Studio.Using simple conversational prompts, creators can ask the tool to generate a tailored thumbnail based on their video’s topic. From there, creators can fine-tune specific visual details, such as adjusting colour schemes, shifting layouts, or refining graphic elements by chatting with the assistant.
Article Summary: Custom thumbnail options for YouTube Shorts and conversational AI-generated thumbnails for long-form videos. Changes aim to help creators save valuable production time while boosting viewer engagement and click-through rates. YouTube Partner Program creators can now upload fully custom thumbnail images for their Shorts.

Article Title: Intel rebounds after ‘difficult times’, reports its fastest revenue growth in 15 years
Article Text:
Data center AI and manufacturing drive surge



Intel reported its fastest revenue growth in 15 years, thanks to booming demand for personal computers and artificial intelligence (AI) data center chips. Revenue for the quarter ending in June jumped 25% year-over-year to $16.1 billion – surpassing Wall Street expectations. The chipmaker also projected current-quarter revenue between $15.8 billion and $16.8 billion, signaling continued momentum.“AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute, and as we continue to execute, Intel is well-positioned to capture sustainable growth,” said Intel Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan, highlighting strength across both chip design and factory operations, as per The Financial Times.The strong performance marks a major comeback for the US chipmaker, which faced severe financial uncertainty just a year ago before receiving strategic backing from the Trump administration in its push to restore domestic semiconductor manufacturing.Intel’s turnaround was powered by a massive spike in demand for central processing units (CPUs), which are increasingly critical for running AI “inference” applications alongside specialised graphics processors (GPUs):While data Center and AI revenue soared 59% to $6.3 billion, well above analyst projections of $5.6 billion; Intel-designed chip sales reached $15.1 billion, beating Wall Street estimates of $13.6 billion.Intel's contract chip manufacturing division generated $5.8 billion, a 31% increase from the prior year. Adjusted net income reached $2.2 billion for the quarter.Under standard GAAP accounting, Intel reported a technical net loss of $11 billion due to accounting volatility tied to escrowed shares from its federal investment deal, which are treated as future obligations.Buoyed by its accelerating growth, Intel raised its 2026 capital expenditure budget from $18 billion to $20 billion and forecast elevated spending through 2027 to outfit its advanced manufacturing facilities.Tan has since secured multibillion-dollar investments from Nvidia and SoftBank, and announced plans to work with Elon Musk on his “Terafab” manufacturing project, all while pursuing company-wide cuts.Intel aims to compete with Nvidia and AMD with its own AI accelerator chip later this year and is seeking to lure big manufacturing clients such as Apple away from TSMC.
Article Summary: Revenue for the quarter ending in June jumped 25% year-over-year to $16.1 billion – surpassing Wall Street expectations. The strong performance marks a major comeback for the US chipmaker, which faced severe financial uncertainty just a year ago.Intel’s turnaround was powered by a massive spike in demand for central processing units (CPUs)

Article Title: Google’s Waymo signals end to Uber deal as companies clash over safety, dirty cars
Article Text:
Waymo's robotaxis carrying passengers in Atlanta, expanding Uber partnership

Waymo-Uber’s ‘blame game’ over routing, dirty cars and bus incidents



Google's sister company and autonomous vehicle unit, Waymo, is reportedly exploring options to exit its partnership with Uber , signaling a deepening rift between the two tech giants as they fight for control over the future of ride-hailing. Citing multiple people familiar with the matter, a report by The Financial Times said that Waymo has held internal discussions about severing its current agreements with Uber, which manages robotaxi rides in major hubs like Austin and Atlanta.The self-driving leader is said to have already notified Uber that it intends to launch its own independent service in those markets starting in January 2028 when its current contract permits.The move marks a shift from 2023, when the companies first joined forces in Phoenix.As Waymo accelerates its expansion across the US, the two companies have increasingly transformed from partners into rivals, with one insider noting they are now “pursuing diverging objectives”, the report said.The relationship has reportedly strained after both companies lodged mutual complaints regarding service quality, safety and operational headaches.While the Alphabet division has questioned the cleanliness and routing of their vehicles and criticised Uber's routing algorithms, Uber has raised issues like bus incidents.In one notable incident in Atlanta, dozens of Waymo vehicles clogged a residential cul-de-sac, which is an issue sources attribute to Uber’s vehicle management. Uber has pushed back, citing unsustainable financial terms and complaining that Waymo's vehicles suddenly go offline during bad weather. In December, Uber formally wrote to Waymo after several robotaxis passed stopped school buses in Austin.The friction has already led to a partial breakup. In May, the two companies allowed their original partnership in Phoenix to lapse.Beyond day-to-day operations, the two companies are locked in a high-stakes lobbying battle to shape state and federal robotaxi laws to benefit their respective business models, The Financial Report said. Uber has lobbied for rules mandating “hybrid networks”, which are platforms that mix human drivers with autonomous cars. In New Jersey, Uber proposed regulations requiring any robotaxi platform to ensure that human drivers fulfill at least 85% of all rides during a three-year pilot program.
Article Summary: Waymo-Uber’s ‘blame game’ over routing, dirty cars and bus incidents has strained the relationship. The two companies are locked in a high-stakes lobbying battle to shape state and federal robotaxi laws to benefit their respective business models.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bill Gates: Don’t compare yourself with anyone in this world. If you do so, you are insulting yourself
Article Text:
Motivational quote by Bill Gates

What Bill Gates’ quote means

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates is known for building one of the world’s biggest tech companies, but he’s also known for sharing simple life lessons. One of his most quoted quotes is “Don’t compare yourself with anyone in this world. If you do so, you are insulting yourself." Even years after he first said it, the message continues to connect with people because it speaks about something almost everyone experiences — comparing themselves with others.The quote is a reminder that everyone’s life is different. People grow up in different families, attend different schools, receive different opportunities and face different challenges. That's why comparing your journey to someone else's journey is often unfair.What works for one doesn’t work for another.When Bill Gates said that comparing yourself with others is like "insulting yourself," the tech billionaire is encouraging people to value their own abilities and progress. The quote means one should not decide their own worth by looking at someone else's achievements.In today's world, it is easy to fall into the habit of comparing yourself with others. Social media shows people celebrating promotions, buying homes, travelling to new places or reaching personal goals.At work, people compare salaries and job titles. Students compare exam results, while entrepreneurs compare the success of their businesses. Over time, these comparisons can make people feel that they are falling behind, even when they are making steady progress in their own lives.The quote also highlights that success looks different for everyone. Some people achieve their goals early in life, while others take longer. Some build businesses, others choose careers in science, education, healthcare or public service. There is no single timeline for success, and comparing yourself with someone on a completely different path often creates unnecessary pressure.
Article Summary: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates is known for sharing simple life lessons. One of his most quoted quotes is “Don’t compare yourself with anyone in this world. If you do so, you are insulting yourself” The quote is a reminder that everyone’s life is different.

Article Title: China's DeepSeek pauses new fundraising days after founder Liang Wenfeng's AI remarks go viral
Article Text:
DeepSeek was founded in 2023

DeepSeek pauses fundraising after founder's reported comments go viral

Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek has paused its second fundraising round just weeks after raising a record $7 billion, reports Bloomberg citing people familiar with the matter. The move comes days after comments widely attributed to founder Liang Wenfeng about China's AI industry and its competition with the US spread widely online. Prospective investors were verbally informed that they would not be signing investment agreements in the coming days as expected. While the fundraising process has been put on hold for now, discussions remain ongoing and the company could choose to restart the deal at a later stage, the people said.According to people familiar with the discussions, DeepSeek decided to suspend the fundraising partly because Liang was frustrated by online reports about comments attributed to him during meetings with investors in the company's first funding round.Bloomberg News said it has not verified the authenticity of the posts, which reportedly contained a transcript of Liang's meeting with unidentified investors.Chinese media outlets, including Yicai, reported this week that Liang discussed China's continued gap with the US in artificial intelligence and the company's reliance on Nvidia chips for AI development. The company had been seeking to raise at least 10 billion yuan in the second round at a pre-money valuation of at least 480 billion yuan, according to an earlier Bloomberg News report.At the same time, DeepSeek has started preparing for an initial public offering and could file for an IPO as early as this year. Founded in 2023 and owned by hedge fund Zhejiang High-Flyer Asset Management, DeepSeek has become one of China's most closely watched AI startups. Its AI model, launched last year, drew global attention by showing that advanced AI systems could be built using fewer computing resources despite US export restrictions on advanced chips.
Article Summary: DeepSeek pauses fundraising after founder's reported comments go viral. The move comes days after comments widely attributed to founder Liang Wenfeng about China's AI industry and its competition with the US. Prospective investors were verbally informed that they would not be signing investment agreements in the coming days as expected.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos: "If you double the number of experiments you do per year, you're going to…”
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos



"If you double the number of experiments you do per year, you're going to double your inventiveness."

Understanding the hidden meaning behind today’s quote



The hidden value of trial and error



Why experimentation matters in everyday life



Lessons hidden inside the quote



Real progress comes from testing ideas, not just planning them.

Practical experiments often uncover insights that are impossible to predict in advance.

Innovation is built through repeated effort over time rather than a single brilliant idea.

The more approaches you explore, the more likely you are to discover effective solutions.

Unsuccessful attempts provide valuable information that guides future improvements.

Trying to eliminate every risk can also eliminate opportunities for meaningful breakthroughs.

Each experiment, whether successful or not, contributes to better decisions and stronger outcomes.

Why the message still feels relevant



Beyond trial and error: Learning with purpose



Innovation is often presented as the result of rare moments of inspiration or breakthrough ideas. Yet people who build successful companies frequently describe it in a far less dramatic way. New products, better systems and unexpected discoveries usually emerge after a long series of attempts, many of which do not work as planned. That pattern can be seen across science, engineering, business and creative work alike. The willingness to try something without knowing the outcome is often what separates steady progress from standing still. Jeff Bezos has spoken about this approach throughout his career, arguing that the volume of experiments matters just as much as the quality of any single idea.At first glance, the statement sounds almost mathematical, but it is not intended as a literal formula. Bezos is pointing towards a simple principle: fresh ideas are usually the result of repeated testing rather than isolated flashes of brilliance.Every experiment produces information. Sometimes that information confirms an idea. Other times it reveals flaws, unexpected customer behaviour or entirely new opportunities.Even unsuccessful attempts contribute to future decisions because they reduce uncertainty. A person or organisation that runs more experiments naturally creates more chances to discover something valuable.The quote also challenges the habit of waiting for certainty before taking action. If every decision has to feel safe before it is tested, the number of experiments remains low, and so does the opportunity to learn.Most innovation follows an uneven path. Early versions of products are refined again and again before they become successful. Scientists test hypotheses that fail. Writers produce drafts that are never published. Engineers discard prototypes that cannot solve the original problem.Each attempt narrows the search for a better solution.This way of thinking changes how failure is viewed. Rather than treating every unsuccessful outcome as wasted effort, experimentation treats it as part of gathering evidence. The important question becomes whether the experiment produced useful knowledge, not simply whether it achieved the desired result.There is also a practical reason for running many small experiments instead of a few large ones. Smaller tests tend to expose problems earlier, allowing adjustments before significant time or money has been invested.Although Bezos made the comment in the context of innovation and business, the underlying idea extends well beyond technology companies.A student preparing for examinations may discover better revision techniques only after trying several study methods. An artist may develop a distinctive style through years of discarded sketches. A chef often refines recipes through repeated adjustments rather than getting everything right on the first attempt.The same pattern appears in everyday problem-solving. People rarely find the most effective approach immediately. They improve by testing different options, observing the results and making gradual changes.Modern workplaces increasingly rely on rapid testing, whether through software updates, product design, marketing campaigns or scientific research. Digital tools have made it easier to gather feedback quickly and adjust ideas before committing to larger changes.The same approach has become common in education, healthcare and public policy, where pilot programmes allow organisations to evaluate new ideas before expanding them. Rather than assuming a single plan is correct, many institutions now rely on evidence gathered through controlled trials and gradual improvements.For individuals, the message remains equally practical. Careers are changing more quickly than in previous decades, making adaptability an important skill. Experimenting with new ways of learning, working or solving problems often provides better guidance than relying solely on prediction.Some people interpret the quote as encouragement to pursue endless ideas without direction.Experiments are most useful when they are deliberate. They begin with a question, test an assumption and produce information that shapes the next decision. Running random trials without reflection does not automatically increase inventiveness.Bezos' observation is less about quantity for its own sake than about creating a habit of continuous learning. More thoughtful experiments expand experience, reduce uncertainty and make genuine innovation more likely over the long term.
Article Summary: Innovation is built through repeated effort over time rather than a single brilliant idea. The willingness to try something without knowing the outcome is often what separates steady progress from standing still. Jeff Bezos argues that the volume of experiments matters just as much as the quality of any single idea.

Article Title: As US government announces new visa restriction policy under Immigration and Nationality Act, it says it is an efforts to dismantle overseas criminal networks that have defrauded Americans of billions
Article Text:
New visa restriction policy’s link to President Donald Trump’s executive order

Chinese criminal networks in spotlight

Recent enforcement actions

The US government has unveiled a new visa restriction policy under the Immigration and Nationality Act, aimed at dismantling overseas criminal networks accused of defrauding Americans of billions of dollars. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently announced the measures stressing that it will apply not only to individuals directly involved in cybercrime but also to their immediate family members. He also emphasised that the administration is deploying “every tool at our disposal—sanctions, prosecutions, asset seizures, extradition requests, and international cooperation” to dismantle these networks and impose costs on perpetrators.The announcement made by the US government builds on President Donald Trump’s March executive order prioritizing prosecutions of cyber-enabled fraud and directing agencies to strengthen tools against transnational criminal organizations. The order warned that countries tolerating such schemes could face sanctions, visa restrictions, foreign aid limits, and expulsion of complicit officials. Trump described cybercrime as “draining American families of their life savings” and highlighted losses of more than $12.5 billion in 2024, with seniors hit hardest.As reported by Epoch Times, Rubio’s statement pointed to Chinese transnational criminal organizations as orchestrators of “pig butchering” scams, in which victims are lured into fraudulent investments through fake online relationships. These groups allegedly defrauded US citizens of at least $10 billion in 2024, while fueling corruption, money laundering, and human trafficking. American children have also been targeted in sextortion scams, causing severe harm to families.The Treasury Department in June sanctioned 35 individuals and entities linked to Cambodia’s Prince Group network, accused of running scam compounds using trafficked labor for cryptocurrency fraud. The Justice Department indicted the group’s chairman and moved to seize billions in bitcoin. Losses from cryptocurrency investment fraud alone reached $7.2 billion in 2025, according to FBI data.Rubio underscored that the visa restrictions are part of a broader campaign to protect Americans from predatory schemes. “By restricting visa issuance to those who are responsible for or complicit in these criminal enterprises, we are sending a clear message: The United States will go after those who prey on our citizens,” he said.

New York continues to lose high-income residents

Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky on Mamdani's rent freeze

According to Internal Revenue Service (IRS) data for 2022-2023, Manhattan attracted the largest number of new tax filers in the United States but still lost about $922 million in adjusted gross income because many high-income taxpayers left and were replaced by lower-earning newcomers.Other parts of New York City also saw significant outflows. Queens recorded a net loss of more than 17,000 tax filers, while the Bronx lost more than 16,000. Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on why he doesn't see an AI bubble bursting anytime soon, says ‘this time it’s different’
Article Text:
Jensen Huang says the world needs an entirely new layer of AI infrastructure

Jensen Huang says he is not worried about Nvidia customers spending on chips

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently said that he does not believe AI boom will end anytime soon, arguing that the current wave of spending is driven by a major shift in computing infrastructure rather than hype. Speaking in an interview with Axios co-founder Mike Allen, Jensen Huang said the AI industry is still in its early stages and demand for AI chips is backed by the need to build a new generation of computing systems. He said the semiconductor industry is not facing the kind of demand cycle that has led to previous boom-and-bust periods."The bubble will burst someday," he said, adding that it will not happen anytime soon because the AI infrastructure buildout is still in its early days."This time is different because this is not demand driven," Huang said during the interview. "This time is different because it's not seasonal. It's not demand driven means seasonal-demand driven. This is industrially driven, meaning the fundamental technology of computers is changing."Jensen Huang said the world now needs an entirely new layer of AI infrastructure, which will require far more chips than are being produced today.He estimated that the industry will need to become five to 10 times larger over the next decade.During the interview, Jensen Huang also dismissed concerns that heavy AI spending by major technology companies could become unsustainable. Several large cloud providers have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to build AI infrastructure, with some turning to the bond market to help fund those investments.Jensen Huang said he is not worried that Nvidia's customers are borrowing money to buy its chips because the shift to AI represents a long-term change in computing."So this future is a whole new way of doing computing that's fundamentally different than the past, and we need a lot more computers," he said.Huang added that AI is already generating profits for companies such as Anthropic as more customers adopt AI agents and other advanced tools. He described the technology as being at an "inflection point," where increased investment is helping improve productivity and expand AI adoption.He also argued that shortages of chips, land, electricity and construction workers are slowing the pace of expansion in a positive way, giving the industry more time to build the infrastructure needed before supply catches up with demand."We basically are constrained in every single direction, in every single way," Huang said. "That constraint is good. That constraint is what holds the system back. So that gives us plenty of time to go build out these infrastructure."
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says he is not worried about Nvidia customers spending on chips. He said the semiconductor industry is not facing the kind of demand cycle that has led to previous boom-and-bust periods. He estimated that the industry will need to become five to 10 times larger over the next decade.

Article Title: ‘How else are people going to learn’: MIT research scientist warns companies replacing Gen Z with AI for entry jobs risk a costly mistake
Article Text:
Andrew McAfee, a research scientist at MIT questioned how organisations expect future professionals to develop if entry-level jobs disappear.

Entry-level hiring plays a role in future workforce development

Young job seekers remain concerned about AI

Companies that replace Gen Z workers with artificial intelligence (AI) in entry-level roles could be creating long-term workforce challenges. Speaking to Harvard Business Review, Andrew McAfee, a research scientist at MIT and co-lead of the university's Initiative on the Digital Economy, questioned how organisations expect future professionals to develop if entry-level jobs disappear.“How else are people going to learn to do the job except via on-the-job learning and training apprenticeship? That’s how you learn to do difficult knowledge work is by helping somebody who’s good at that with the routine stuff. And when we put too much automation in that too quickly, we lose that apprenticeship ladder,” McAfee said.McAfee argued that reducing entry-level hiring does more than shrink the current workforce.He said it disrupts the pathway through which employees develop the skills needed for more complex roles over time.He also said companies risk losing a generation that is already comfortable working with artificial intelligence. According to a Deloitte study published in November 2025, 76% of Gen Z respondents reported using a standalone AI tool, the highest share among all generations.“There is a big demographic falloff. As people tend to get older, we tend to be more set in our ways and less willing to try crazy new things like AI,” McAfee, who is also the co-founder of Workhelix, said.“So if you’re pulling back on your entry-level hiring, you are probably sacrificing future opportunities to learn and the skilled people of the future. You’re also turning off the spigot of the most enthusiastic power users of AI in your organisation,” he added.McAfee's comments come as many graduates report growing concerns about the impact of AI on employment. According to Handshake's Class of 2026 Network Trends report, entry-level job postings on the platform are down 2% year over year and remain 12% below pre-pandemic levels.Meanwhile, the unemployment rate for college graduates aged between 22 and 27 stands at 5.6%, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.A Monster survey also found that nearly nine in 10 graduates from the Class of 2026 are concerned that AI or automation could replace entry-level jobs, compared with 64% in 2025.Some executives have echoed those concerns. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had previously said AI could eliminate up to half of entry-level white-collar jobs before later softening that prediction.However, a recent Goldman Sachs analysis suggested younger workers have historically adapted more effectively to technological shifts. The report found college-educated young workers generally experience earnings losses around half as large as other displaced workers over the decade following job loss and are more likely to move into occupations that complement emerging technologies.“Contrary to current concerns that the costs of AI will fall especially hard on new graduates, younger workers have actually been able to adjust more flexibly through occupational mobility and skill upgrading in the past,” the report said.
Article Summary: Andrew McAfee, a research scientist at MIT, questioned how organisations expect future professionals to develop if entry-level jobs disappear. He said companies risk losing a generation that is already comfortable working with artificial intelligence. According to a Deloitte study published in November 2025, 76% of Gen Z respondents reported using a standalone AI tool.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai: "We don't get to choose the world we graduate into but…"
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai



"We don't get to choose the world we graduate into, but we do get to choose how we frame our circumstances.” : Commencement address to Stanford's Class of 2026.

What the quote means



What Sundar Pichai's quote teaches about career resilience and adaptability



About Sundar Pichai



Key lessons from Sundar Pichai 's quote



Not all hardships carry with them an underlying advantage. As mentioned in the quote, there are instances wherein life can really be tough.

Differentiate between the incident and the reaction to it. While you may not always be able to determine what is going to happen to you, you can definitely choose how to respond to it.

Take note of the things that you still have control of. External factors may be out of your hands but your attitude and actions need not be.

Do not define yourself according to a few temporary obstacles. A tough start or unexpected roadblock need not affect your future at all.

Failure is also not permanent. Success should not cause complacency as life is always a process of adaptation.

Perspective determines future actions. The way that you see a particular situation can affect your confidence in taking further action.

Why the message still feels relevant



A common misunderstanding



Words often stay with people long after the moment they are spoken, especially when they capture an experience that feels widely shared. Quotes from influential leaders frequently gain attention because they offer a different way of looking at familiar challenges rather than simple advice. Google CEO Sundar Pichai 's reflections have often centred on education, technology and adapting to change, making them relevant to students, professionals and anyone facing an uncertain future. One of his most widely discussed observations encourages people to think about what remains within their control when circumstances cannot be changed. This message is not only about optimism but more about perspective, resilience and making thoughtful choices in unpredictable situations.The quote is related to how individuals structure and interpret their experience and not what the actual experience is all about. While the facts may remain the same, the interpretation itself can change and determine future actions.When interpreted from such a point of view, what Pichai says is not urging individuals to ignore difficulties or make problems smaller than they actually are. Getting fired, graduating during tough times or venturing into a new sector can still be very hard no matter what your attitude is.It only means that the initial reaction does not have to define the entire situation.This is important because the interpretation usually determines future actions. One person may interpret uncertainty as a sign that there are no more opportunities left to be found anymore while another will interpret the same uncertainty as a sign that things have changed and new opportunities are bound to arise.Many careers no longer follow predictable patterns. Entire industries evolve within a few years, while new occupations appear that barely existed a decade earlier. Graduates entering employment now often face repeated periods of adaptation rather than a single lifelong profession.Against that backdrop, the quote feels less like career advice and more like an observation about flexibility. It recognises that circumstances will continue to shift. Preparing for change involves more than acquiring technical knowledge; it also requires the ability to reassess situations without becoming trapped by first impressions.That does not eliminate disappointment. Expectations can still be disrupted. Plans can still fail. The quote leaves room for those realities while arguing that people retain some influence over the story they tell themselves about what happens next.Sundar Pichai is the Chief Executive Officer of Google and its parent company, Alphabet. He studied metallurgical engineering before continuing his education in the United States, where he earned degrees from Stanford University and the Wharton School.He joined Google in 2004 and worked on products including Google Toolbar and the Chrome browser before taking responsibility for Android and several other major services. Over time, he became one of the company's most senior leaders and was appointed Google's CEO in 2015, later assuming leadership of Alphabet as well.Throughout his public appearances, Pichai has often spoken about education, access to technology and adapting to periods of rapid change. His speeches usually place less emphasis on predicting the future than on developing habits that allow people to respond when the future proves different from expectations.Technological developments in artificial intelligence, automation, and digital communication keep on transforming the nature of labor markets. The graduates often get contradictory predictions concerning the skills that will be valued and professions that will become extinct.In light of this unpredictability, Pichai’s statement does not make predictions but rather draws attention to the way of thinking that will be valuable irrespective of what technology prevails. Being open-minded and ready to think differently might be more sustainable than being sure of the chosen career path.This approach works outside the labor market as well. People encounter a number of unexpected things that happen not according to their plans, whether they concern economics, family, or any other aspect of life. The first understanding of the situation is not always the final one.The quotation is sometimes mistaken for a call to positive thinking, but its meaning is more restrained than that. Pichai is not suggesting that difficult situations disappear if viewed differently, nor is he implying that success depends entirely on attitude.Instead, the statement distinguishes between events and interpretation. Circumstances remain real and sometimes harsh. The way people understand those circumstances, however, can affect whether they remain fixed in place or begin searching for different possibilities. That balance between accepting reality and choosing a response is what gives the quote its lasting relevance.
Article Summary: Sundar Pichai is the Chief Executive Officer of Google and its parent company, Alphabet. His reflections have often centred on education, technology and adapting to change. The quote is not urging individuals to ignore difficulties or make problems smaller than they actually are.

Article Title: Workplace software Monday.com cuts hundreds of jobs; read CEO Eran Zinman's 'layoff email' to employees
Article Text:
Here's the full memo sent by Eran Zinman, Co-founder and Co-CEO at Monday.com, to employees

Hi everyone,

Why are we making this change?

A flatter organization

More autonomous teams

A new go-to-market model

For the people leaving monday.com

For the people staying

We are deeply confident about our future

Israeli workplace software maker Monday.com is laying off hundreds of employees as part of a restructuring plan. The software company announced the layoffs in an Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing. The company said it is reducing its headcount by 20%, or about 630 staff, to “support a leaner, more focused operating model” as it concentrates on its AI Work Platform.In the SEC filing, the Tel Aviv-based company said that it has "initiated a restructuring plan." In a memo sent to employees about the layoffs, posted to LinkedIn, Eran Zinman, a cofounder of the company, claimed that the move was not about replacing employees with technology."We are not making this change to protect what we have. We are making it to go all in on what monday.com can become," the memo reads.Over the past nine months, we have shifted our core vision moving from managing work to doing the work for our customers, with people and AI agents working together in one workspace. This has required us to change our product, our strategy, and how we serve our customers.But it became clear that changing our strategy and product is not enough.The organization we built for our previous chapter is not the organization that fits the new AI era. Today, we are announcing the very difficult decision to reduce our global workforce by ~20%, affecting around 620 people.This is the most painful decision we have made since founding monday.com - yet we are certain it is the right one. We made it. We own it. And we take full responsibility for it.The people leaving are talented colleagues and friends. They helped build this company, support our customers, and create a culture we are deeply proud of. We are incredibly grateful to them, and we know that nothing we say can lessen the impact this will have on them and their families.We are not making this change to protect what we have. We are making it to go all in on what monday.com can become.We entered a new era where AI is transforming the role of software, creating the greatest opportunity our industry has ever seen.We have a new market to capture. Without a fundamental change in how we operate, we will not be able to compete and win that market.To fully realize this opportunity, and ensure monday.com is positioned to lead in this landscape, we need to move faster, execute more decisively, take on new challenges, respond quickly to market changes, and empower people in the company to create greater impact. Some of the things we are changing in monday:- We are reducing management layers, creating more empowered teams, and enabling faster decision-making.- We are moving from teams with many dependencies to smaller groups with broader ownership and greater authority to execute.- Our new offering is opening a new market, and that market requires us to work differently. New and existing customers increasingly expect deeper implementation support as they adopt AI. We will work more closely with customers, increase our on-site presence, create new roles, and adapt many existing ones.Improving margins was not the purpose of this decision. We intend to reinvest the vast majority of the savings in our people, our products, AI, and future growth.Thank you. Thank you for all your hard work, for the significant impact you have made, for caring so deeply about monday.com, and for always being willing to help and lend a hand. We know this is part of our culture, and it is something we consistently hear from everyone who interacts with people at monday.com.We want to be very clear: this decision is not a reflection of your performance, your contribution, or your value. It is the result of a management decision about how to structure the company for its next chapter.We are committed to supporting you through this transition with care, respect, and meaningful assistance. We will do everything we reasonably can to help you find your next opportunity, and we will provide you with a generous support package.To companies that are hiring: we recommend these people wholeheartedly. They are exceptional professionals and teammates, and we will help connect them with organizations looking for outstanding talent.It is not easy to be part of such a significant change or to see colleagues and friends leave so quickly. We understand how difficult this will be. We also owe you clarity about what this change means.The change is not about asking fewer people to do the same amount of work. We are making real choices about what we will stop doing. We will simplify how we work, remove unnecessary friction, and give teams more authority to make decisions.The company that comes out of this change will have clearer priorities, fewer layers, faster decisions, and greater ownership.Our path is very clear to us. This is a change we have chosen to make, and we are taking full responsibility for it. We have never seen such a significant opportunity in software, driven by such exciting technology.Nothing gives us more confidence than seeing how new and existing customers are responding to our new offering, and seeing adoption of our AI products accelerate.Every week, we see more evidence that our strategy is the right one. Customers are embracing our new vision, adoption of our AI capabilities continues to accelerate, and our confidence continues to grow.Our momentum is strong, and we believe we are on the right path to success on a massive market opportunity.To ease the uncertainty around this we will send all employees an email message within the next hour, followed by a personal call from one of your managers.For all managers - we know how difficult it is to process this personally, even as you continue to lead your teams. We have every confidence in your leadership and know you’ll approach these conversations with the care, clarity, and respect that define our culture. Thank you for being there for your people during this transition.Thank you,Roy & Eran
Article Summary: Israeli workplace software maker Monday.com is laying off hundreds of employees as part of a restructuring plan. The company said it is reducing its headcount by 20%, or about 630 staff, to “support a leaner, more focused operating model” as it concentrates on its AI Work Platform.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes his first-ever post on Twitter; says: I am sharing a letter signed on why ...
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang joined Twitter in June this year

Here’s the full text of letter Jensen Huang shared in his first Twitter post



"In the 1980s, early open-source software pioneers challenged the prevailing belief that software would advance only if companies kept tight control over their code. This movement pushed for a transparent ecosystem where developers around the world could study, modify, and improve software. Software developed by the open-source community now supports most of the internet and underlies systems used by the world’s largest technology companies, as well as the U.S. military and federal agencies conducting scientific research, cybersecurity, and other critical missions. Open source did more than lower the cost of software; it created a shared foundation of knowledge on which generations of American engineers and entrepreneurs built their institutional sovereignty.

The United States now faces a similar choice with artificial intelligence. Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector. This is essential for creating opportunities for innovation and prosperity across the country. It requires expanding access to AI, encouraging competition, robust application layers, and giving Americans greater control over the technology they rely on. Open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure—are an important part of that foundation because they make advanced AI more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.

Open weights expand access to the AI economy. Startups, established businesses, universities, and public institutions can build on advanced models without training one from scratch or paying frontier model prices for every task. Open weights let every organization match the right model to the right job at the right cost, reserving frontier-scale capability for genuine frontier problems and running efficient, specialized models everywhere else. That discipline is what will make AI economically sustainable as its use scales into the billions of everyday tasks.

America

wins the AI era by diffusing it into the workflows of factories, hospitals, farms, classrooms, and main street businesses.

Open weights also strengthen competition and competition is what keeps the gains of AI broadly shared rather than concentrated in a few hands. By allowing many organizations to build, adapt, and deploy advanced models, open weights create rivalry not only among model developers but across cloud chips, applications, and services. That competition spurs innovation, drives down costs, and distributes the benefits of AI broadly across our economy. Open weights also give customers greater control. As organizations invest in AI, they want to know that they will not become locked into a single provider or lose the knowledge and capabilities they build over time. Open weight models help provide that assurance by allowing organizations to control their own data, evaluate and adapt models to their own needs, and deploy them wherever their business requirements demand. And as organizations create value with AI, open weights allow them to own that value through self-improving models, specialized capabilities, and accumulated knowledge that drive American sovereignty and prosperity.

To be sure, open weights carry real and distinct risks. Once released, the weights are beyond the original developer's control, and modified versions are difficult to trace or reverse. But the right response to this risk is not to prohibit open weights. In a world where cybersecurity attackers use advanced AI, defenders need access to models with comparable capabilities so they can detect, simulate, and respond to emerging threats. Open models broaden defensive capability, increase transparency, and allow vulnerabilities to be discovered and remediated across many teams.

In fact, openness may be one of the most important paths to AI safety and security. Relying solely on closed models is not inherently safe: they can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect. And concentrating advanced AI capabilities behind a small number of closed models compounds that risk. It results in a small number of single points of failure, weakens competition, and leaves critical technology in the hands of a few providers. Open weight models, on the other hand, allow a broad community of researchers and developers to examine their behavior, identify vulnerabilities, develop safeguards, and improve them over time. Just as open-source software demonstrated that transparency can be more secure than obscurity, AI safety may depend on giving more people the ability to test and strengthen the models on which society relies. It allows for rigorous benchmarking and evaluation, red teaming, and protections tied to real and demonstrated harms rather than assuming that closed systems are safer by default.

A strong AI ecosystem is not a foregone conclusion. Policymakers have an important opportunity to act. This includes expanding access to compute for startups and researchers, investing in shared training assets (datasets, tools, evaluation frameworks), and keeping the frontier plural by avoiding premature restrictions on open models that stifle competition or drive innovation overseas. These measures must also look at how strong application layers can expand sovereign use of AI across the economy.

In shaping this ecosystem, policymakers should be careful not to conflate legitimate model development techniques with misappropriation. Distillation, or the practice of using one model's outputs to help train or improve another, is a widely used technique for model improvement, evaluation, and validation. It reflects a long tradition of learning from, building upon, and improving existing technologies, a tradition that has helped drive innovation since the rise of the open-source software movement. By contrast, unlawful efforts to extract value from closed models raise legitimate concerns. Those concerns should be addressed through targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping restrictions on techniques that play an important role in AI innovation.

The age of AI can be one of prosperity. With the right choices, open weight AI can expand opportunity, strengthen competition, extend American technological leadership, mitigate risk, and ensure that the benefits of this extraordinary technology are shared broadly across our economy. That future is worth building, and the United States should lead in building it."

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made his first-ever post on Twitter (now X) on July 24. In the post, Jensen Huang shared an open letter on why open models matter. The letter, signed by Nvidia and 24 other companies, warns the US not to repeat the mistake of over-restricting technology the way some feared for open-source software in the 1980s. It argues that open-weight AI models should be preserved as a foundation for American leadership. “Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector,” the letter says, adding “This is essential for creating opportunities for innovation and prosperity across the country”.Sharing the post, Jensen Huang wrote:“For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter. AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country.Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty. The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models."
Article Summary: Jensen Huang: U.S. will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector. It requires expanding access to AI, encouraging competition, robust application layers, and giving Americans greater control over technology.

Article Title: ‘Shortest day of 2026’ is set to come this month, though this tiny time change in Earth’s day may look ‘small’, how this 'milli-seconds shift' is threatening GPS and satellites
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representational purpose only

What is actually happening on July 26



Why Earth’s rotation changes



1.33 milliseconds per century: Climate change connection with GPS, space missions



This Sunday, July 26, will be the shortest day of 2026. However, the difference is so tiny – just 0.65 milliseconds – that no one will notice. This time is less than the blink of an eye, less than the time it takes a camera flash to fire, and life will carry on entirely undisturbed. But behind that ‘flicker of time’ lies a story that scientists say should concern all of us. The Earth's rotation is altering in ways that are unmatched in at least 3.6 million years, and climate change is the reason.According to the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS), the organisation responsible for keeping global time, Sunday's day will measure approximately 0.65 milliseconds shorter than the standard 24 hours, or 86,400 seconds. That makes it the shortest day of the year so far. But here is the thing: it is actually less extreme than recent years.In 2025, the shortest day, recorded on July 10, came in at 1.37 milliseconds shorter than standard. This year’s figure is roughly half that, suggesting Earth's recent spell of unusually rapid rotation may be easing. The data comes from TimeAndDate.com, which reported the IERS's mid-July predictions, and it tells a story of a planet whose rotation is shifting in ways that are small in the short term but significant over decades and centuries.Earth’s speed of rotation is not fixed. It fluctuates constantly due to a complex web of factors, including ocean currents, atmospheric pressure and the gravitational pull of the moon that shifts in how mass is distributed across the planet.Time on Earth is based on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which is designed to closely follow the planet’s rotation. When the rotation drifts significantly, timekeepers add or remove “leap seconds” to keep UTC aligned with the actual position of Earth.This is where the story becomes genuinely alarming and where a fraction of a millisecond starts to carry real weight. New research from the University of Vienna and ETH Zürich, published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth earlier this year, has found that Earth's day is currently lengthening at a rate of approximately 1.33 milliseconds per century. That rate is faster than anything seen in at least 3.6 million years of Earth’s history.As climate change melts glaciers and polar ice sheets, the water they contain moves from the poles toward the oceans, redistributing mass across the planet. Earth slows down when mass moves away from its rotational axis toward the equator.Researchers reached this conclusion by analysing fossil remains of benthic foraminifera and using advanced machine learning techniques to reconstruct how day length has changed over millions of years.Modern satellite navigation systems, including GPS, Galileo and GLONASS, depend on extraordinarily precise knowledge of Earth's rotation. When users ask the phone for directions or a pilot uses GPS to land a plane, the system is calculating the users’ position based on where Earth is pointing at any given millisecond. If Earth's rotation drifts faster than the models predict, those calculations drift too.Space missions face similar challenges. Navigating a spacecraft requires knowing exactly how Earth is oriented, which means errors of even a fraction of a millisecond in rotation data can translate into meaningful positional errors at the distances involved.Global timekeeping systems are also affected. The decision of when to add or remove a leap second depends on accurate tracking of Earth’s rotation. As the rate of change accelerates, those decisions become more complex and the margins for error shrink.The changes are currently manageable. But as the rate of lengthening continues, the pressure on the systems that underpin modern navigation, communication and timekeeping will grow.
Article Summary: Sunday, July 26, will be the shortest day of 2026. But the difference is so tiny – just 0.65 milliseconds – that no one will notice. But behind that ‘flicker of time’ lies a story that scientists say should concern all of us. The Earth's rotation is altering in ways that are unmatched in at least 3.6 million years, and climate change is the reason.

The Microsoft co-founder loved fast Porsches, drove them hard, and collected enough tickets that traffic cops became a regular fixture of his early years. At one point his driving record got bad enough to put his license—and reportedly his freedom—on the line.So Gates did something unusual. When Seymour Rubinstein, one of Microsoft's biggest competitors, showed up expecting a business meeting, Gates told him the meeting was moving to traffic court. Rubinstein, the founder of MicroPro and the man behind the hugely popular WordStar, ended up coaching his young rival on how to avoid jail time and keep his license.Gates's love of speed went back to Microsoft's earliest days. He owned a green Porsche 911 and pushed it constantly. During the company's move from Albuquerque to Seattle, he reportedly drove the Porsche past 100 mph and got caught more than once. One time his radar detector was useless—police were clocking his speed from an aircraft overhead.The traffic court episode is documented in, the 1992 book by James Wallace and Jim Erickson. Rubinstein arrived for what he thought was a normal Microsoft meeting, only to be told he was heading to court to watch Gates answer for his driving.Rubinstein wasn't just any competitor. WordStar was one of the first commercially successful PC applications, and he later claimed it held 72% of the word-processing market going into 1984. Microsoft had released Word for MS-DOS on September 29, 1983, putting the two men on a direct collision course.But they went back a long way. Rubinstein was about 21 years older than Gates and had signed an early OEM deal with Gates and Paul Allen during his IMSAI days. They talked often and traded advice. Gates wanted to fight his ticket on a technicality—owning a radar detector was legal, he argued, and he felt the officer had treated him unfairly for spotting it. Rubinstein knew that wouldn't fly with a judge. He told Gates to apologise, promise to bin the radar detector, and swear he'd stop speeding. Gates listened, and dodged the worst of it.Gates later tried engineering a fix. He bought a sluggish brown Mercedes diesel—no working radio, so he could think while driving—treating it as a self-imposed speed limiter and a test of discipline. It didn't work. Fortune reported in 1986 that he kept collecting tickets even in the slower car. The Mercedes eventually died from an engine failure tied to an oil oversight, and Gates went back to a Porsche capable of roughly 155 mph. The problem, it turned out, was never the car.

During the company's move from Albuquerque to Seattle, he reportedly drove the Porsche past 100 mph and got caught more than once. One time his radar detector was useless—police were clocking his speed from an aircraft overhead.

Article Title: As Oracle loses $498 billion in less than 10 months, why credit rating agency S&P has identified Sam Altman's OpenAI as a 'key credit risk' for Larry Ellison's company
Article Text:
Why S&P calls OpenAI a 'key credit risk'

Why Oracle's credit rating was downgraded

Here’s what S&P said about OpenAI being a ‘key security risk’ for Oracle

Oracle has lost about $498 billion in market value in less than 10 months. Recently, credit rating agency S&P Global Ratings identified Sam Altman 's OpenAI as a "key credit risk" for the company. In a report explaining its decision to downgrade Oracle's credit rating, S&P said the software giant's aggressive push into AI infrastructure has made it increasingly dependent on a handful of large customers, with OpenAI standing out as the biggest concern. The agency estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of Oracle's $638 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO), warning that if the ChatGPT maker is unable to meet its financial commitments, Oracle could be left with costly data centre leases and weaker cash flow.S&P said Oracle's AI infrastructure business now carries much higher risks than its traditional software business because it requires massive upfront investments in data centres, chips and long-term leases before generating returns.According to the agency, OpenAI represents around 50% of Oracle's $638 billion RPO, making the Microsoft-backed AI company one of Oracle's most important customers. As mentioned anove, S&P warned that OpenAI's ability to honour its contracts depends on continued growth in the AI industry, its ability to raise external funding and whether its AI models remain market leaders."If OpenAI were unable to pay Oracle, we believe Oracle could be left with massive data center leases that it might be unable to exit or have to re-lease to new tenants under less-favorable terms," S&P said.The agency added that it is monitoring OpenAI's financial commitments to data centre operators and chip makers as an indicator of its future financial strength.S&P lowered Oracle's long-term credit rating to 'BBB-' from 'BBB', saying it had underestimated both the scale of Oracle's AI investments and their impact on the company's financial profile.The agency expects Oracle's cloud infrastructure business to grow from 27% of revenue in fiscal 2026 to nearly 60% by fiscal 2028. While that supports future growth, S&P believes it also exposes Oracle to greater financial risk because AI infrastructure requires heavy spending before profits are realised.Oracle has guided capital expenditure of $90 billion to $95 billion for fiscal 2027, far above S&P's earlier estimate of $60 billion.The rating agency now expects Oracle's free operating cash flow deficit to widen to nearly $42 billion in fiscal 2027, compared with its previous forecast of negative $24 billion.OpenAI remains a key credit risk. We estimate that OpenAI makes up roughly half of the $638 billion in RPO. OpenAI’s ability to meet its contractual obligations and raise external financing will be contingent upon AI tailwinds continuing and its models being market leaders. If OpenAI were unable to pay Oracle, we believe Oracle could be left with massive data center leases that it might be unable to exit or have to re-lease to new tenants under less-favorable terms. As a proxy for OpenAI’s future prospects, we’re tracking OpenAI’s financial commitments to data center operators and chip makers to gauge its overall financial exposure and its market share among enterprise and consumers.
Article Summary: S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle's long-term credit rating to 'BBB-' from'BBB. S&P said Oracle's aggressive push into AI infrastructure has made it increasingly dependent on a handful of large customers. The agency estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of Oracle's $638 billion in remaining performance obligations.

Article Title: As Europe Scientists struggles with heatwave, scientists find alternative to air conditioning, including advances in materials that passively cool buildings
Article Text:
For representative purpose

Why air conditioning cannot be sustainable solution



Solution: Sending heat directly into space



As record-breaking heatwaves sweep across large areas of Europe and Asia, city planners and homeowners are searching for ways to stay cool. While air conditioning remains the go-to fix in nations like the US, Japan, and Australia, scientists warn that installing AC units in every home is an unsustainable trap. Researchers have now highlighted breakthroughs in passive cooling materials, including specialised paints, hydrogel films and radiative coatings, that can lower building temperatures without relying on electricity or overloading power grids.Cooling buildings already accounts for nearly 10% of global electricity consumption, according to a recent review published in Nature Reviews Clean Technology. By 2050, the electricity required to cool indoor spaces is projected to jump by 210%, with greenhouse gas emissions from air conditioning expected to triple.Beyond energy consumption, scientists point out three critical flaws with traditional air conditioning. The first is grid strain that will be caused by massive spikes in AC usage during extreme heatwaves. The second is heat ‘Vicious Loop’. Standard split-system AC units cool indoor rooms by extracting heat and dumping it outdoors.This raises ambient outdoor temperatures in cities, driving higher demand for even more air conditioning.The third is the economic gap. The report says that up to 100 million families across developing regions in India, Mexico, Indonesia, and Brazil will remain unable to afford AC units by 2040, despite having electrical access.“Air conditioning can be life-saving for people at high risk, but the technology has severe drawbacks. We need solutions that don't compound the problem,” explains Matthaios Santamouris, an architecture researcher at the University of New South Wales.Passive cooling technologies require minimal to no power, using advanced material design to regulate building temperatures. The options include automated sun-tracking blinds and window slats that are already common in commercial towers. However, the most promising breakthrough involves passive radiative cooling.This tech takes advantage of the "atmospheric window"—a specific spectrum of heat waves (8 to 13 micrometers) that can pass directly through Earth's atmosphere and escape into space.The first is radiative paints that are infused with microscopic silica and aluminum oxide spheres to scatter solar radiation. This reflects 97% of solar energy and lowers surface temperatures by around 5.26 degrees Celsius.The second solution is evaporative hydrogel films that absorb moisture at night and evaporate water during hot daytime hours while repelling heat. These are claimed to reduce direct sunlight surface temperatures by about 7 degrees Celsius.The researchers say that applying these high-tech coatings to roofs and exterior walls effectively turns whole structures into self-cooling units.“We really need to tackle this problem from different angles,” says urban climatologist Negin Nazarian. By blending advanced materials with smart design, cities can keep residents safe during extreme summer heatwaves without worsening the global climate crisis.
Article Summary: By 2050, the electricity required to cool indoor spaces is projected to jump by 210%, with greenhouse gas emissions from air conditioning expected to triple. Researchers have highlighted breakthroughs in passive cooling materials, including specialised paints, hydrogel films and radiative coatings.
